events/1315_amnistia/phases/0/narrative: The thirteenth year of exile. Florence declares an amnesty — and a letter arrives in the little courtyard where he lodges. Dante is almost fifty. He has missed home for thirteen years.
events/1315_amnistia/phases/0/instructio: Read the terms of the amnesty, then hear what the people around him say.
events/1315_amnistia/phases/0/npcs/0/dia: Master Alighieri, good news! The city is pardoning its exiles. Let me read you the terms —
“One: pay a fine. Two: put on the penitent's robe and the paper hat. Three: walk with the procession to the Baptistery of San Giovanni, and make an offering to the patron saint for your sins.”
Walk it once, and you can go home. Sir, plenty of men beg for this and never get it.
events/1315_amnistia/phases/0/npcs/1/dia: On the parchment, the commune's seal he knows so well. The words “penance” and “offering” are written out especially neatly.
The Baptistery of San Giovanni… where I was baptized. They want me walked through the streets as a sinner, back to the place my life began.
events/1315_amnistia/phases/0/npcs/2/dia: Sir, Grandpa says you look south every single day.
What's over there, in the south?
events/1315_amnistia/phases/0/npcs/3/dia: Father. The sentence takes in your sons as well — Jacopo and I are on the exile list too.
Just take it. The paper hat comes off after one day. I want to go home.
events/1315_amnistia/phases/1/situation:
Thirteen years on, a letter from Florence:
pay the fine, wear the penitent's robe, be marched through the streets confessing — and they will let you back.
events/1315_amnistia/phases/1/options/0/: Accept. Pay the fine, walk in the procession, go home — his wife and children again, and his own city to grow old in.
events/1315_amnistia/phases/1/options/1/: Refuse. Rather grow old and die under someone else's roof.
events/1315_amnistia/phases/1/sameNote: You guessed it. So here's the next question: what made him think that was worth it?
events/1315_amnistia/phases/1/diffNote: He didn't take it. Thirteen years, one chance to go home, and he didn't take it.
events/1315_amnistia/phases/1/reveal:
“This is not the road home for me.
If there is another road that costs Dante nothing in honor and dignity, I will walk it without a moment's hesitation.
If there is not — then I will never set foot in Florence.

Can I not see the sun and the moon and the stars anywhere else?
Can I not think the sweetest thoughts unless I first shame myself in front of my own city?
Bread, I will not go short of, anywhere.”
— Letter XII
events/1315_amnistia/phases/1/consequenc:
A few months later Florence changed the sentence: Dante and his sons, beheading. (Before that it was burning.)

He never went back. He died in Ravenna in 1321 and was buried there.
For six hundred years afterwards Florence asked Ravenna for his bones, again and again, and never once got them.
The tomb built for him in the church of Santa Croce is empty to this day.
events/1315_amnistia/phases/2/transition:
A few months later Florence changed the sentence:
Dante and his sons, beheading.
(Before that it was burning.)
events/1315_amnistia/phases/2/announceme: Boccaccio closes his lecture notes and says nothing for a long moment: “Fellow Florentines. Our city shut its best son out twice — the first time with fire, the second time with a paper hat. And he answered with a whole Paradiso: there is only one crowning he will take. If the Divine Comedy ever brings him home, he will stand at the font where he was baptized and put on the laurel.”
events/1315_amnistia/phases/2/dufu_react:
“If this holy poem can beat the cruelty that shuts me out of the sheepfold —
I will come back with another voice, in another fleece,
and at the font where I was baptized I will take the laurel.” (Paradiso XXV)
quiz/1315_amnistia/quizzes/0/question: In the 1315 amnesty, what did Florence ask an exile to do in exchange for coming home?
quiz/1315_amnistia/quizzes/0/options/0: Swear loyalty to the Blacks' government
quiz/1315_amnistia/quizzes/0/options/1: Pay a fine, walk in the procession in a penitent's robe and paper hat, and make an offering at the Baptistery
quiz/1315_amnistia/quizzes/0/options/2: Hand over everything he had written
quiz/1315_amnistia/quizzes/0/options/3: Serve three years in the army
quiz/1315_amnistia/quizzes/0/explanation: The terms were: pay a fine, put on the penitent's robe and paper hat, walk with the procession to the Baptistery of San Giovanni and “make an offering” — humiliated in public, as a sinner. Dante's answer, in Letter XII: “This is not the road home for me.”
quiz/1315_amnistia/quizzes/1/question: After Dante refused the amnesty, what did Florence change his sentence to?
quiz/1315_amnistia/quizzes/1/options/2: Beheading for Dante and his sons (before that it was burning)
quiz/1315_amnistia/quizzes/1/explanation: A few months after he refused, Florence changed the sentence to beheading for Dante and his sons — his sons were pulled in with him. He had already written his answer in the letter that turned it down: “Bread, I will not go short of, anywhere.”
quiz/1315_amnistia/quizzes/2/question:
At the start of Paradiso XXV, Dante writes down the only crowning he will accept:
“I will come back with another voice, in another fleece, and at the font where I was baptized I will take the ___”
quiz/1315_amnistia/quizzes/2/explanation: Paradiso XXV: “If this holy poem can beat the cruelty that shuts me out of the sheepfold… I will take the laurel at the font where I was baptized.” That font is the Baptistery of San Giovanni, where he was baptized in 1265 — he died still waiting for it, and Florence owes him that laurel to this day.
